utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before we begin with the evidence, I'll just give two short decisions on applications for protective measures. On the 17th of January, the Prosecution filed a partly confidential motion for protective measures for Witnesses 35 and 50, requesting that each be assigned a pseudonym and being granted image and voice distortion during their testimony. They attached a confidential annex setting out the circumstances supporting the request for protective measures. On the 18th of January, another partly confidential motion was filed for protective measures in relation to Witness 62. The Prosecution requested that this witness be assigned a pseudonym and be allowed to testify with image distortion, and it set out the reasons for protective measures in a confidential annex. The Trial Chamber notes that the Defence has stated that it does not object to the granting of these motions. In light of all the circumstances, including the submissions made by the Prosecution and the contents of the annexes, and also in light of the relevant provisions of the Statute and the regulations, the Chamber grants these two motions. We may now proceed, Ms. Isailovic, with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Welcome. Good morning, Mr. Overgard. I'm Ms. Branislava Isailovic. I'm with the Paris bar. I'm a counsel of Mr. Dragomir Milosevic, accused in this case. I'll ask you a few questions that have to do with the examination-in-chief yesterday. I will also use a statement that you made to the Prosecution's investigators on September 8, 1995, April 29, 1996, and April 30, 1996. So, first and foremost, do you remember those statements which have been compiled into a single declaration?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember those, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: We have few -- we had a few technical problems this morning, and of course we gave notice to the opposing party of this, and because of these technical problems we've prepared hard copies of these statements and I will ask the usher to please circulate these hard copies to the Chamber and, of course, to the witness. Now, first I'll ask my assistant to display a map on the screen. This is the map that was developed by the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to have to interrupt, but we don't have the transcript, Judge Harhoff and myself. We have it now. Do you? There's something which you have to do. Judge Mindua just did it for me. Judge Harhoff is still without the transcript, but please go ahead. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'm sure that this gave enough time for the map to be actually displayed on the screen now. This is the map that takes a bit long to be uploaded.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: A few questions now maybe before the map is displayed, a few questions. Major, you've been in the military for 18 years before you went to Sarajevo; is that true? So you were in the military for 18 years before coming to Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you talked about your military training. So first you went to the military school; is that it?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And then you went through a training session in Finland for this mission, for this Bosnian mission.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I went to the training in May 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: During this training course you studied how to make investigations that are required after incidents of shelling and sniping.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: As well as how to gather intelligence and how to analyse craters; is that it?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So this is my question: I'd like to know whether in the training course you also studied technical data regarding the weapons that could be used by artillery units.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we had obviously some lessons with technical datas, and I used to recognise them and have them in my head, but now they're out.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So I guess this was just a refresher course, because you already had information and you had courses on the weapons used by artillery. It was a refresher course.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a course specially for the mission, yes, for the UNMO job.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this wasn't exactly my question. So could you assess yourself as being an expert regarding artillery weapons?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not artillery weapons. I'm educated for the anti-tank weapons. But we have -- we used in the support unit mortar 107 millimetres. I knew that one. And 80 millimetres [Realtime transcript read in error "188 millimetres"], I knew that one before. I'm not an expert on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So regarding those anti-tank weapons, the air bomb -- do air bombs fall into that category?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I see it says 188 millimetres on line 10. It should be 80 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Well, thank you. Now, the map is being displayed. So this is a map regarding the territories where you were stationed. So could you show us Hrasnica on the map, if you please. Could we please move -- display -- scroll forward, if the map could be scrolled upward a little bit.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have the Hrasnica area here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. My assistant is telling me that normally it's the usher that's supposed to do this. So could you please scroll up, Mr. Usher. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Major, please, could you show us Hrasnica on this map.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's this area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Are you absolutely sure?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: This is Hrasnica where you were stationed? I mean, you were there for quite a while.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. I didn't see the airport area here. You have Hrasnica here at the foot of Mount Igman. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I don't doubt your goodwill. It's just that the map isn't very legible. So please could you also locate approximately the direction where Ilidza was, because you were mentioning Ilidza yesterday. So could you tell us --

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ilidza is this direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And please, I'm sure you know Lukavica, or maybe you know it.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this here, around this area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. What about -- so this is Lukavica. Do you know anything about this? Do you know who was in control of this part of the territory?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a Serb-controlled area I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, the first area that he mistakenly marked as Hrasnica, it's occurring to me that it's still on the map as being marked, and maybe if he could put a line through it so that we know it's not applicable.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand he has to erase it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So on the map could you please show Vojkovici, if this rings a bell of course. Does Vojkovici ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the name is there, but I'm not too sure with the ...

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was in control over that area?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a Serb-controlled area, and ...

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And, in your recollection, is it close to Hrasnica? Is it the part of Sarajevo that's close to Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. It's -- I'm not sure ...

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You're sure of that? And Grlica, that place name, does that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Grlica, yes, also, but on the map I was -- I don't know if I have it --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Would it be close to Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Grlica, it was not one --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Grlica.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Grlica, it rings a bell also. I don't remember, but I think it has to be in this area, then. We had the Famos factory here, and the name and place now on this map, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: To the right of Hrasnica you pointed at something. Is that what you think is that place we're looking for? Because I see that you put a mark.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This is the -- I don't remember the name of the place where we had this Famos factory, where we had a lot of firing from into Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was in control over that part of town?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a Serb-controlled area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And, in your recollection, were these densely populated villages? I apologise. Were these villages that were populated also by civilians?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think there was. I wasn't into that specific area. So if there were civilians there, I can't say, because there was a lot of firing from that area, from the Famos factory building, and we were not allowed in there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on to what you did in Sarajevo, rather, in Hrasnica, which is part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So first could we give -- could we tender and give a number to this map that has been marked by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D14, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Before the map is put into evidence, could I ask my learned friend to mark, or have the witness mark, these various circles and lines that are on the map for sake of clarity of the record. Perhaps put a capital H by Hrasnica, a capital L by Lukavice, and so on, or whatever makes sense, because otherwise, I fear that several months from now we won't remember what these marks mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let that be done.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead. Should I ask questions about this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. I'm instructing the witness to do as counsel just suggested.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So A, you've been noting a few letters. An A, you put an A on the map?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The A is for Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And B is for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Famos factory area. And C is Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And lastly, can we put a D by Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The direction of Ilidza more than anything, because you can't really see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a 65 ter -- could I have the document 2824. It's a 65 ter document. I apologise, Your Honour, our client would like to send us a word, so could the guard please give us that little word that our client wants to have sent over to us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not really working that way. It's our assistant that's going there. So let's move on quickly to something else. We're all fine now with the map; right? And this map that has been marked has been tendered into evidence; right? The 65 ter 2824, that's been done. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Witness, you said that your job was to investigate incidents that have happened in Hrasnica. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you right in your testimony yesterday and in that written statement, these investigations were always conducted together with local police.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. They've -- we investigated in our way and they had their investigation going parallel. We are not cooperating at all. We often delegated them our resources, because the policeman was an earlier artist, a painter or something, and he had not have -- did not have experiences.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So you were helping local police and giving them all the technical information that you had on the incidents; is that it?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: We only gave them the results and we worked two UNMOs together and helped consult them. They had their own things to do.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is kindly asked to speak into the microphone and not lean forward too much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, we also delved into an investigation which occurred on April 8, 1995, after an incident that resulted from an air bomb being dropped on a house in Hrasnica. That's what -- do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was -- the bomb landed on the 7th and we had an investigation done on the 8th.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood things right, this happened during -- after lunch; right?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Around what time, please?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say the exact clock, but it was sometime on the day because we had to negotiate our way out again, to get back our freedom of movement.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So in France we have lunch around 1.00 p.m. So is it after 1.00?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it's around 1.00, because we had lunch around 12.00 normally.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I'll quickly move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please display the other -- the other 65 ter map, 2823.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: This is a map that was shown to you yesterday. It's a bit more detailed, at least when it comes to Hrasnica. So on this map, yesterday you showed us the house where you were stationed at the time. Do you remember that? You located the house.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and I have -- when I saw the pictures from this -- what pictures we had some problems with yesterday, I located the house to the far east for you. West, I believe, against Ilidza. We had our accommodation just between the two marked spots and into the mountain area. I think it was ...

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: We'll correct that. So just for clarification, if I've understood you right, Sierra Sierra 2 was this house. Sierra Sierra 2 was exactly that house where you were stationed.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. We had a house -- the team location in -- I don't know if I understand you right. In that house I was -- the houses are not on the map, as we saw yesterday, where we were stationed. But the station team building was a house of -- where we rented, civilian house.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But did you call that -- did you call that Sierra Sierra 2?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was Sierra Sierra 2 until Christmastime, and then it -- then it was renamed to Sierra India 1, or Sierra Igman 1, because we were the Sierra Igman team.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think if we could please display the map. It's not on the screen yet, so I'll move on to something else, a question that doesn't require a map.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So we'll talk about this investigation that was conducted on April 8, 1995. The explosion occurred on the 7th, in the morning; April 7th, in the morning --

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: -- is that it? Did it wake you up?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- we were actually in the living-room after breakfast, because that day I was supposed to go into Sarajevo for a meeting, but -- so when the explosion occurred, I was in the living-room together with one of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty, you no longer wish to make your point?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can I just -- can I just put a question for clarification, because I was a bit unsure about the answer that Mr. Overgard gave to your question, counsel; namely, the question of whether it was Sierra Sierra 2 which was destroyed by the bomb. That was not the case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. I believe that we understood each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So you are saying, and you remembered, you actually remember, whether it was a quiet day or whether there had been already sounds of fire, of explosions.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. So far that morning it was quiet. No small-arms fire, nothing. So this just --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And the day before, the 6th?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 6th was -- I don't remember, but I don't think we had any special investigation on the 6th.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But since you're a fact witness here, can you tell us, if you remember, whether this period was rather quiet? Or how would you describe that period?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: In April, it -- or March, late March and April, the fighting was getting more intense. It was increasing, the firing, day by day.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: When you heard the explosion, I understand that you immediately went out and you went on site. Now, what I'd like to know is how you guessed exactly where the explosion had taken place.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was very close to our accommodation and so we saw it. We first tried to phone the civilian police, as we did, to inform them that we wanted to investigate. There was no answer in the police station so we went first past the site and went to the police station. There was nobody there so then we went back to the site.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So if I sum up what you've said, you went on site, you went to the site where the explosion had taken place. You were able to note and to see that the house had been completely destroyed. It's the house that we saw yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And you saw that there was great damage on eight other houses there.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were several other houses damaged as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, this was not mentioned, but by reading your written statement at page 2 -- I believe that everyone has this statement now, and you, too, Witness. Do you have your statement?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And here you say that you did not see the body of the woman who was killed.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at the site, no. I saw her on the morgue only.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Then we see in your statement - and you repeated that earlier on - then you walked to see the name of someone, Hakija, Hasan Efendic.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Efendic, I think that was the name, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Hasan Efendic. He was the local police inspector, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Then together with Mr. Hasan Efendic you went back to the site.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me now roughly how much time this took, this going from the site of the explosion to the police station and back? How long did this whole thing take?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not walked. We used our patrol vehicle. That's a Toyota, so -- but it --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: How long did it take, then? It was quicker.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That took approximately I believe -- from the explosion till we came from the police station and into the site again, 20 minutes, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You're saying that the commander of the 4th Motorised Brigade of the Bosnian army, I suppose it was the 1st Corps, you said that he had already come to the site and that you saw him when you came back from the local police station.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. He arrived to the site as we were looking around to get the overview of what the damages are. So I was at the moment just looking over their wall we saw on the picture yesterday that was broken, and I saw some feet in the pile of bricks and stones there, inside the house. That's when we were ordered away from the site.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: How did you know that this was the commander of the 4th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had been in meetings with him earlier, and it was the -- our interpreter of the corps who was calling me and saying that he was here and wanted to talk to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Then you said that this gentleman, the commander, gave you an order. By the way, do you remember his name?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at the moment. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You said that he ordered you to leave the site of the explosion, and you went to your base. We saw earlier on that the base was this house that we've identified. Now we have the map displayed on screen. Can you see the map?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And at the same time we'll correct the mistake we made yesterday. So can you please show us on the map this place where you were accommodated.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can try. I have to push some buttons. Okay. Our accommodation is more or less from this site here, I believe. I, yesterday, pointed up in the area of the centre of Ilidza -- or Hrasnica, I mean. So we are very close. Yeah, I said here, more or less, our house.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please immediately tell us where the incident took place, where the explosion took place? Can you mark that on the map, please.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's already marked as number 6 here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I'd like to have a number for this map that has been marked by the witness, and maybe we could write an A next to Sierra Sierra 2, or Sierra India.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please, Witness, write the letter A next to Sierra Sierra 2.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You've said, and that's on the transcript, that number 6 -- am I right in saying that number 6 marks where we find the destroyed house?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you left when you were ordered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please let the officer give the map a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That becomes Exhibit D15, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So you said because you were ordered to -- you left because you were ordered to do so by the commander of the 4th Motorised Brigade of the BiH, and you went to this house that is marked with an A on the map. And if I remember correctly, but you can correct me if I'm wrong, you said that the explosion took place around 9.00. Then, if we think that it took you about one hour to do all the things you've described, we could say that you went back to the base around 10.00 or 10.30. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can be right, yes. Unfortunately, I lost my diary and so on due to some hijacking later on in the duty. But it can be something like that, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Once you arrived at your base, you stayed there until 7.00 p.m., if I understand correctly.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And in that house there were two other soldiers with you - soldiers or officers, I'm not quite sure what their rank was - two members of the FreBat, the French battalion; is that right? And that is to be found in your statement, at page 3 of your written statement, at the top of the page, in the first paragraph. So you are saying: "[In English] There were three BH soldiers guarding the house. When we wanted to leave our accommodation they would not let us. Some people from FreBat arrived."

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had a visit from FreBat, two officers and one interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These three soldiers we mentioned earlier on, they were already standing before your house when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were. They came there at the same time as we arrived. They was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Were you escorted by anyone to your accommodation, to your base, or was it just the two of you? Because, if I understand correctly, you were with your British colleague there.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was together with my British colleague and one interpreter, and we went or drove to our accommodation on our own. As we arrived there, there were these soldiers outside, and they came at the same time as us.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So, if I understand you correctly, there were four military personnel there from the United Nations; the two of you plus two members of the FreBat, in that house. And the house itself was under the guard of these three BiH soldiers. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the team location, so I believe that most of the team, except for those on leave and so on, were in the house. So the whole team was gathered in the house that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: On top of the four of you, so the two of you plus the members of the FreBat, and then all your colleagues, all the other colleagues of the team.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And all of you were prevented from moving freely for a great deal of time. You were prevented to do so by the three BiH soldiers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I would really like to know how they managed to keep you inside in that way, to prevent you from going out, to sequester you.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, when we heard that they are armed, we are not. The FreBat soldiers were armed, but still we had no mandate to force our way. This has to be solved on a headquarters level with the LOs and commanders. So we are not provoking them as enemies. We are still peacekeepers, not peacemakers. So for us, we respect that. And, yeah, using the phone, using lines to the PTT building and the headquarters, yeah, that was the main thing we could do. And no one will risk to be shot.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I fully understand. But we can confirm now that between around 11.00 and 7.00 p.m., you were locked in that house with all the members of your teams and all the other people, and in order not to cause any provocation to the members of the ABiH, you decided that you were going to obey their orders.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We obeyed and stayed inside the house, tried to send our interpreter out to talk with them if they -- to hear if they had received any new orders about how long and so on, yes. We wanted to go out, of course, to investigate, but we did not -- as I said, we did not provoke them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So at 7.00 p.m., and you say that yourself, and that's all -- it's still on the 7th of April, 1995; right?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thus between 11.00 and 7.00 p.m. you stay in the house, and at 7.00 p.m. you left the house.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Me and Mr. Calum Gunn went out to the site, yes, in the afternoon, or in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You went to the site but you did not conduct your own investigation, did you?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not. We just had a look around, see how it was, because it was starting to get dark and there was no use for us then to investigate any further that night.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Was this site protected? I mean to say, were people prevented from entering the site?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was marked and clearly stated that no one should enter. And there were guards also in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Then you went to your base, and we can read in your statement - and I'd like you to give us some further explanation about this - where you said that you were again prevented from going out of the house, and you were only able to leave the house the next day after lunch; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And who prevented you from leaving the house?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The BiH soldiers were back outside our house, the police soldiers. We had to wait until this meeting had taken place with the liaison officers, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So you were there just to help them take stock of what had happened following the incident that allegedly had been provoked by the army of Republika Srpska; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I have the text on the screen here? Because I only have two mikes now. So I can be sure I'm understanding the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we are -- we are not there for -- only to take stock, but we are there to patrol, report what we see, what we are doing during --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: That was not absolutely not the word I used. [In English] Try to see that in English. You were there to help -- to help them.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are there to -- not to help them. We are there to observe and report what is happening and do that job for the UN. So we are still impartial in the conflicts wherever we go.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since you're impartial, could we conclude that that's the reason why you were maltreated the way you were, because you were impartial?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, I think they wanted to get these experts from Sarajevo, bomb/explosive experts from Sarajevo, and they didn't trust us to do the right investigation in this case. This was so big that never had -- things like that had never happened before.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But on the 8th of April, after lunch you still went to the site, and in your statement you said that you conducted the investigation together with the Bosnian police.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just as they were doing their investigation, we still -- they had a language which we did not understand. So we did ours, just to see what there was. That was the main reason. We had to clarify what caused all this damage.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So according to you, the investigation took place on the 8th of April, after lunch.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's when we investigated this, and I think if we can get hold of this report from that -- the team reports from that day, we will find that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'll deal with this with another witness, because, according to you, the investigation took place on the 8th of April, 1995, because, you see, we have a report with another date, with a different date. But you're not aware of what happened on the 7th because you were held captive in this house. That's why I'm not going to deal with it further with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, madam, but I have a few questions I would like to put to the witness about the same matter. Please tell us, Witness, with regard to this particular incident, if I understand you correctly, on the 7th of April, between 8.00 and 9.00, between the hours of 8.00 and 9.00, there is an explosion. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you went there, you went to the site, on two occasions. I'm summing up what happened then. When you went to the site on the second occasion, you took note of a number of damage. A house had been completely destroyed, and eight other houses had been damaged. There's a dead body there. And people are wearing camouflage uniforms, or there is at least one camouflage uniform you see there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was this one inside the house, under the bricks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The commander of the 4th Brigade prevents you from going back to the site. So you are, so to speak, held captive or confined, if I use the words of the Defence counsel. And when you go back to the site on the next day, you do not find any of these traces, any of these things. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We don't -- there were no bodies left there, but there still were some remained, shrapnels and so on from the bombs and from the rockets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now let me move on to my questions. According to you - because you're a specialist and we know that you are competent in this matter - according to you, the damage you saw on the second occasion, when you went to the site on the second occasion, was this damage due to or caused by the air bomb, or was this damage caused by ammunition that would have been placed or located in the destroyed house or the surrounding houses? And this is just a possibility. Now let's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say that this came from inside the house, because all the bricks were drawn into the house. So this explosion had been outside the house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The camouflage uniform you're talking about, can we say about this camouflage uniform that there was at least one member of the armed forces in the house or around the house? Can we deduct that from the camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As we didn't -- we only saw his feet, I don't know if he was a soldier, because a lot of people use these camouflage trousers. It was, I think, something common and cheap for them to get. But anyhow, if he's -- if a soldier was at home in his house and so on, he is, according to the Convention, a civilian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now let me move on to my very last question. Could this house have been considered as a military target that could have been targeted by any military force or by the Serbs, for example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot imagine that, no. There were no signs of military flags, nothing outside of that house. It was not different from all the other houses in Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: During the investigation that you conducted on site on the 8th of April, 1995, can you please tell us what method you used in order to determine, to identify, the direction of the bomb? On the 8th, were you in a position to establish already that this was an air bomb?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, due to the shrapnels we found, and so on, this had to be -- we found -- in the discussion between Calum Gunn and me, we found that this was an old English air bomb that the shrapnels had to come from. And then we also saw the tails and the engines from the rockets, we saw the remains of them. So for the direction, we had to rely on the -- more or less, to the witness statements and the fact that the windows only in that direction against Ilidza, along that street, were broken; not in front of the bomb, only backwards. So something had gone -- and that also makes the sound we heard just before the bomb came or exploded, it sounded for us that it came from that direction, because there was a noise like an aeroplane coming very low from that direction and into us. That's why we were nearly on the floor when the bang came.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: In your house you throw yourself to the ground. That happened on the 7th. But all the shrapnel, the rockets, you saw it on the 8th; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. We saw some of it when we were there on the site, just after -- before we were detained in our house, ordered to go back. But we could not at that time take a close look to see what it was. But that was on the 8th where we saw more remains. They also had gathered more of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But what did you see on the 7th, then?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 7th, we saw some, I would say, bits and pieces of bombshell, and we saw that it has to be -- at least of the one of the engines. But at that time we could not see what it was to be sure. That was only on the 8th. And then we can start to take notes and make drawings of the site and the houses around.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure. It may be a problem of translation, but you said that on the 7th you were not sure that you had seen all these pieces, or am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 7th, we just -- we saw there was, as I say, bits and pieces, shrapnels, metal pieces, but we were not able, or we did not also have the time to have a closer look at it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you didn't look at them very closely, but just in the way you looked, you were able to see these bits and pieces, these small pieces; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The smaller they are, the -- you could say some 20, 30 centimetres, some of them. But, as I say, we could not stay. We still had a question at 7.00 in the evening: What was this?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Indeed. In your statement, page 3, first paragraph still, right at the end of it, I mean the first paragraph that starts with the words "When we came ..." there you said that you were able to go in the evening to the site: [In English] "The first day we could not find anything, no fragments."

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, due to the fact that it was getting dark when we were there, the evening. That was after the meeting with the security officer. We did not collect anything or could not see any special things at that time. But what we saw anyhow, it has to be -- just stay there where it was, not to be picked up.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday and today you mentioned information gathered from eyewitnesses. Did you obtain this information on the 8th?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would be on the 8th we got that information. The 7th we were not given information at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: These eyewitnesses, were they English speaking or were they people who spoke the language? The local people, I mean.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the local people and the statements came through our interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: However, did you yourself write down the summary, the minutes of the statements yourself, or was it done only in what is called here B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The summary of this one, or what ...

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You see, you relied -- and you said it yourself. In order to establish from which direction the air bomb came, you relied on the testimony of eyewitnesses. So you obtained this on the 8th through your interpreter. Therefore, you were able to ascertain the contents of their testimony, and I asked you whether this was put down in writing, and whether it was done in English or not at all, to make it possible for you to see what was in there.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was -- these statements were taken by, I don't remember, one of the team members, and I don't remember who it was. But that together with the fact that the damage of the windows and so on went in one direction, and what this witness said just -- that makes it. So that was the conclusion we could take on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can I ask you something? Without the statement from the witness, would you have been able to determine the direction from which the bomb came?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We only then could assume, from what I mentioned, this window, that it had come from that direction. I think -- I don't believe that we had other indications. So that would -- that will be the conclusion anyhow, that it came from that direction. But I'm not so much an expert on this type of weapon that I can say exactly, to say that exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Yes, I was planning to put the same question as you just did, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And we heard that you were no expert in this type of weapon, but, Witness, somehow yesterday you described the weapon. You said that it is a weapon you cannot control. I mean the air bomb, that it is difficult or impossible to control. Is it right? Is that what you stated?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So as far as this description, I don't know whether you said that yesterday too, but in your written statement, third paragraph, around the middle of the page you said this: [In English] "You have no control after launching the bomb." [Interpretation] Can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said so, and ...

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Again, I mean that is quite obvious. I'm really unable to understand, and I'm no expert at all in matters of weapons. I'm a woman, after all, and I did not do any military service. But my feeling is that, looking into this, as I did last year, I was amazed to see that there were a lot of weapons or projectiles that were launched and that could no longer be controlled. There were a lot of pieces or elements. Yesterday, for instance, we had to stop because there was a storm around. So there are a lot of things or forces that do, if not control, influence the direction, the location. Say, if you take a shell, it's bound to fall. It cannot be controlled once it is launched. Once a mortar shell is launched, it can not be controlled. Am I right or is this totally wrong?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you have launched it, it will go and land. You cannot do anything to stop it or to change the direction. It's not controlled. Today you have weapons you can control, but not weapons like this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So based on your experience in Bosnia, say somebody -- or NATO, say, because towards the end of the conflict NATO became involved in this conflict. Maybe they did have guided missiles, but the air bombs used then, were they the only weapon that could not be controlled once they were launched?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I say, mortars and artillery, grenades, are sent out and you cannot hit some -- hit a bull's-eye with them, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your help on this, because, really, in this matter I don't understand much when it comes to weapons. I can confirm that. Thank you. Very quickly I'll deal with the last subject. It has to do with -- well, we have the map here on the screen, and I'd like you to show everybody the famous headquarters of the 4th Brigade. Yesterday, you mentioned the headquarters of a company. I suppose the company was part of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the company is part of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please show us the headquarters on the map. And then I'll ask for a number and I'd like to tender the map once it's marked. What you're marking right now, what is it? Is that the company?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the brigade headquarters. I believe it was -- it was one of these houses somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Could it be marked as B for brigade, or "QG" in French would be headquarters, brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let it be marked B.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Or HB.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Then you spoke about the company headquarters. Can we see that?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the combat -- yes. Front line. There are some buildings in this area here, I believe it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot go in detail because the buildings are not on the map, so I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: It cannot be seen on the map. Can we scroll down or, rather, scroll up for us to see. Is it possible to scroll it up?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the buildings there are not marked, I think. The normal houses --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I know, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For counsel's benefit, once the witness has marked on the map, it can't be manipulated. So we can either have him -- we can move the map and have him remark, or we'll have to keep the map where it is now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Court Deputy. That was very useful. So we can erase the second marking because it is not accurate. We can keep only as evidence the map showing the location of the brigade headquarters. Can that be done? Can I have a number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can that be done, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. That will be admitted as Exhibit D16.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we can have the map again but without any marking. I hope we can move it up, please, so that the major can see and show us the company headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Can you do this, sir?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only see the general area, and it had a marking up here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this area here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Here, in this area, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: All right. I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we mark this as C? Would that be suitable, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let that be done.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] C for company.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Because I can see the territory of Kovaci which you mention in your statement as being the location where there were four mortars discovered in April. Would you be able to show us the position?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mortars were down there -- in there. In this area here. I can't be more accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please could you mark this location with a 4M?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I shall ask Mr. Court Deputy to give us a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be admitted as Exhibit D17, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Here again I rely on your military knowledge. Could you tell me whether -- in here I've got a ruler, and we have the scale. We can see then in a rather small limited space between the headquarters we've just seen, the brigade headquarters, and then we saw the company headquarters and thereafter the mortars that were discovered but that did exist at a given point in time. It's not a big portion of territory, is it? Some 1 kilometre or 1.2 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I respectfully object to that question. There is a scale on the map. The areas are clearly marked. And to have the witness guess or characterise the distances when it can be calculated precisely from the map will only cloud the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He's in a position, you say, to give the distance precisely?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: More than that, Your Honour. Anyone is in a position to give the distance precisely, because in the lower left of the exhibit that has now been introduced as D17 there is a scale. Therefore, from the green dot that's marked as 6 to the 4M, or to the C, can be calculated precisely, and there is no need to ask the witness to give an imprecise calculation for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Ms. Isailovic, with that in mind, reformulate your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have the ruler in my hand, and I did measure. This is the reason why I'm asking of the witness to tell me whether it is, indeed, roughly 1 to 1.2 kilometres as the distance between the company and the brigade, because from the brigade to 4M it's about 100 to 200 metres precisely. Could the witness, based on his memory - of course, this is not precise; this will be corroborated by further testimony - but on the basis of his recollection, since he was an eyewitness -- that's the only the basis. I'm not asking for exact things. I do agree with the statement made by the Prosecution. I do have my ruler and anybody can calculate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. What is your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this would be guessing here, but I think she said the brigade headquarters. But from the company headquarters to the mortar, which was the closest, and they are still more than a kilometre away from the civilian areas, so it's -- the weapons are not that inaccurate when we are coming to mortars. Within an area, you can say you will hit but not ...

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: This was not my concern right now. My question is as follows: Because we have two headquarters, therefore, I suppose there are soldiers as well, soldiers that move about the headquarters; right?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would say. And there are, of course, forces in a pocket like this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And I guess that there are other military facilities that are necessary to the running of the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: These headquarters were in a civilian house, a normal house, but I think emptied for civilians, as I know. But I can't say that clearly and be sure because I did not go into them myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely. As a military man, I'm asking you this: A headquarters for any unit require other facilities. This is just military logic. You need some warehouse for the weapons you have stored. Were there any other military facilities around the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not as I could see. But I don't know what was inside all the buildings, that is all. I cannot say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Perfect. Very last topic, a minor topic. Yesterday, we had brewing the Belgian weapon, 12.7 millimetres in calibre, in territory held bit ABiH, in Igman; is that right? And you explained that it could not reach Hrasnica but only Republika Srpska-held territory. This is to be found in your proofing notes. Do you remember that? Do you remember your statement yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember most of this. I don't know if you're absolutely right. We saw them first on Igman, the first time, and were not -- and that was BiH forces, yes. That was the sniper gun, the 12.7. Observations of Serbian forces having this weapon, I cannot confirm that. But I know we had had incoming fire from the Serbia area of 12.7.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You are saying that in territory held by the ABiH, that is, Mount Igman, you saw that weapon.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that weapon passing one soldier driving one day, yes. That was I think in March, but I cannot say because, as I say, all my notes are gone.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You can therefore confirm that on Mount Igman and on the road to Igman you also had forces, troops, soldiers, or units of the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course they are using positions in the hillside there from one time, but there was no -- no places I saw they had -- or stayed all the time. And not on the road. The road was used also by the military, yes, for sure, but mostly civilian traffic, white trucks, blue trucks, and so on, and private cars.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: If you wanted to go to Igman or if they wanted to go to Igman, did those soldiers go through Hrasnica? Was that the usual route?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the usual route through Hrasnica. They entered the hillside up to an area called -- on the convoy road, called the bus-stop, and there they collected and went. They were collected by cars and went out into the mountains areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: This would be my next question: This famous bus-stop, it was not a bus-stop, but was it possible from there to use another vehicle to go to Mount Igman?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from there they could -- they were in shelter from direct fire, so they could upload vehicles there and drive up to Igman.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: In your written statement you also mentioned tunnels, and the exit of that tunnel, you said, was often targeted by the army of Republika Srpska. Do you remember where the exit was?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. It was in the -- called the Sokolovici area, outside. Just a couple of houses on the field there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Major, at the time did you know whether the tunnel was used and what it was used for?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They started to dig this hole there. Yeah, it was January, February, something like that. And we passed it very often, the hole they were digging there, just to see what it was, trying to ask the question, What are you doing? And they just told us they were digging holes for collecting water, and so on, a lot of blah, blah, of course, just to lead us off. But in the end they had made this tunnel, yes. But I don't think it was finished before I left.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: We're lucky we know this from other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, how much longer will you be?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, five to ten minutes more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue. Ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Ten minutes will be plenty.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to start where we stopped before the break, so let's go back to the tunnel. You said, and I quote, "We weren't really allowed to look and investigate and find out what was really happening with that tunnel." Is that it?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were not allowed to stay too close there in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And if my memory is right, you also said, regarding the headquarters, that there also you were not really allowed to inspect what had happened in the surroundings. Is that true also?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did think about us entering houses around and the headquarters. We only visit that we had into headquarters was for meetings, and that was different from one day or another, where we were not aware who did the meetings, team leader or someone else. We had -- for our own security, in that area of the company headquarters, we did not inspect or patrol that area too much because of the firing risks. We had incidents there where our car got hit. So, yeah, we did not inspect those houses any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Then around those houses you said that there were soldiers around those houses, that in Kovaci you found mortars. Can you tell us who discovered those mortars?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mortars were discovered by our team. I don't remember who it was. They stood there for a while some days and then they were removed. And they were pointing in the direction west, you could say, to the Ilidza area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So I think, from what I understood you said earlier, you were not really allowed to circulate freely. So you found that by chance, because you weren't really allowed to move around to do your inspections; right?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were -- most of the time, about these incidents we're talking about, we were allowed to go. But into the front line area we had to give the message that we wanted to inspect that. We had three cars in our team; one car regularly on Mount Igman and two cars to do both patrolling and administrative tasks, for getting food, so on. So I would say one car for patrolling more or less the whole time, but then you had the manpower, how many of us left in the team that day. Some were on leave; some were at meetings, and so on. So what you ask for, we had had no restrictions for movement on a daily basis normally. It was a -- we had to -- to go into any special sites close to the confrontation line, we had to give the message to the commander. So sometimes they said -- could say that, No, this will not be secure for you; we don't really want you there. They did not deny us, but we -- of course, as we are UNMOs, we also tried to have a good relationships. We didn't provoke them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: How long did it take before you could -- between asking to go to a place at the confrontation line and then being given the okay? Did it take a few hours, did it take a few days, or what?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be an answer on the phone immediately. So we had an interpreter phoning to brigade headquarters and we got the answer at once so that we could perform our task for that day without further planning.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Did this mean, for example, that you're calling on the phone and immediately you can go to the confrontation line, right after your phone call?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we could go to that area and do what task we were supposed to, if it was normally just patrolling or doing a special task in that area, if it was a sniper accident there or if we had to just stop and have an observation post to see what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. So I'm talking about the confrontation line. That's just for the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the only place we had to -- the confrontation line was one area where we had to just tell them we wanted to go, but otherwise we had freedom of movement. We were driving up and down the convoy road as we wanted. We went to Sarajevo as we wanted. So no problem with that, that we have to go through the Sokolovic, Butmir areas, so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm interested in this: You're saying you have to give -- you have to signal that you're going there. So I'd like to know how long it takes between signalling that you want to go someplace and the moment where you actually arrive in the confrontation line. How long does it take? That's exactly my question.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. As we get the answer, normally we got that answer at once and then we could go, and then it was just the driving time from accommodation to confrontation line and that's not many minutes. So no problem with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: That was my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was my last question, Your Honour, and now I'm done with my cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Isailovic. Before you re-examine, may I take you, Major, back to the question that I had earlier asked. I earlier asked you whether the conclusion that you had arrived as to the direction from which the bomb came could have been made without the benefit of the statements from the witnesses, and your answer was yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It will then be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm just asking. That was the position. You said yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. So I want to ask you: Was that conclusion, in fact, made by you before you had the benefit of the statements from the witnesses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That conclusion was taken by us, by the team, me and Calum Gunn, I believe, and maybe some others during this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Was that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- conclusion noted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe it -- I don't know how it was reported to the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's your practice in relation to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Normally, of course, you have to give the direction, if you have an investigation. So I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It would be noted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And could be found.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And the statements from the witnesses, where would those be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These statements were delivered to our headquarters. Like all papers we were writing, the would deliver them there. So I hope -- from there, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How many witnesses did you examine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This witness was -- I had one, but others had talked with other people, and this was a lot of paper done. And I believe that was Calum Gunn collecting it, so I can't say how many. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Major, I want to start my re-examination at the same point as His Honour Judge Robinson. You mentioned some of the things you used to determine the direction from which this air bomb had come. In your accommodation, did you also hear this air bomb before it landed and exploded?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I mentioned, we were in our accommodation and we heard this sound. Something was coming, like a C130 or something, like an aeroplane coming in. That was just to say I was faced against where the explosion was, but I had it on my left ear and I was on my way down when the explosion came, because this was something not familiar, something new, this sound.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: From the sound, could you tell anything about the direction of travel of this bomb?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We came -- I was inside so that was impossible. But as I had this sound in the left ear, it had to be on the west side of our accommodation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And just for the sake of completeness, what is to the west of your accommodation?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is against the confrontation line with the company headquarter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, you were also asked some questions by counsel for the Defence about military traffic on what is called the convoy road. Do you remember those questions?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And in those questions let me ask this: How far is it from the scene of this air bomb incident to the convoy road?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is quite a good distance from that. I cannot say in metres, but a kilometre or more.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And that question about distances raises the question of guiding ammunition once it has been fired. Again, counsel for the Defence asked you a series of questions about that. Do you remember those?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I want to ask you about three different types of weapons - mortars, artillery pieces, and air bombs. Before it's fired, can a mortar be aimed?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not direct weapons. You are not aiming, but you are giving it a load, a starter to -- an elevation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then you can tell where it's going to land. If you don't have the data about the wind in the higher levels, and so on, you're not sure but this is where you want it to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: So you can make some adjustments --

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: -- so that the mortar falls, shell falls, in the area you want it to fall.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: What about artillery pieces? Can they be aimed?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's the same with them, but they are bigger. There's more explosives in artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: But, again, when you say it's the same, only bigger, do I --

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: They can go for bombing areas, not specific targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And can an air bomb even be aimed as to a general area?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. And then an air bomb, as you mentioned yesterday, does not have a guidance system; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: This type we're talking about here does not have, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And so an air bomb is going to come down, if I'm correct, when the fuel runs out.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Wherever --

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wherever.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: -- wherever that happens to be.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Or it can also be equipped with a timed fuse --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- a timer. So you can predict that somewhere 60 seconds from firing, or something like that, then -- where it can be. That's the only thing you have. That's very inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Yesterday, on direct examination, I asked you if, in your air force career, you had learned what sorts of weapons are suited to different types of battlefield conditions. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Do mortars have uses in different battlefield situations?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mortars are to take out positions mostly, to clear areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: So the answer would be yes, they have a military function.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Artillery, does it have a military function?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And the question I put to you yesterday: Is there any battlefield situation in which an aircraft bomb with rocket engines strapped to it would be the weapon of choice for a commander?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Major, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for giving it, and you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There's a decision which I'll now give on a Prosecution motion for admission of written statements. On the 11th of January, the Prosecution filed a motion for admission of written statements pursuant to Rules 92 bis and ter. The Prosecution seeks the admission into evidence of the statements of, inter alia, Witnesses W35 and W83 pursuant to Rule 92 ter. Yesterday, the Defence indicated that they had no objection to the admission of these statements. The Trial Chamber grants the Prosecution motion insofar as it relates to Witnesses 35 and 83 and admits these statements into evidence upon fulfillment of the conditions set out in the Rule. Mr. Waespi, your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the next witness comes in, the completion of Mr. Overgard's testimony means I am finished with examining witnesses for some time. May I be excused from further attendance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
