utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may begin, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. I just have one point of clarification for this witness. He has a very prominent position back home; he's the Minister of the Interior of his province, and he needs to go back at the end of today. Also, his visa expires. I will lead the witness for about an hour, so before the lunch break, and I really hope that Your Honours, with your questions, and the Defence will be concluding their questions by the end of today, which I understand is 4.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, we'll go on until 5.00, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm much obliged. Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mohatarem. Can you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: My name is Ghulam Muhammad Mohatarem.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what is your current position?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: I'm the Home Secretary of the Government of Sindh, the southern province of Pakistan.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you do have a military career, a professional military career, behind you. Can you very, very briefly tell us the steps in your military career, please.

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: I retired -- I was commissioned in the army in 1971. I served during my service in the tank corps of the Pakistan army. I've been in Bosnia as the chief UN Military Observer. I've also served as a defence attache in Myanmar and Bangladesh. I retired after 33 years of service in 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Mohatarem, you mentioned you were in Bosnia. Can you tell Their Honours the time you were in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: I was there from mid-February till early January, 1995 to 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So that will be February 1995 to January 1996.

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You mentioned that you were the chief UN Military Observer in observe. Can you tell Their Honours what your job was.

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: The job as the chief UN Military Observer was to monitor the agreements that were made between different warring factions, to conduct negotiations with different warring factions, to advise the UNPROFOR commander. While I was there, it was Lieutenant General Rupert Smith. I also had a responsibility towards monitoring the movement of humanitarian convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, who was your direct superior? To whom did you report?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: I reported to the chief UN observer -- chief UN Military Observer for former Yugoslavia based in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Do go on.

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: Since I was placed in Sarajevo in the UNPROFOR headquarters, I had regular interaction with the commander of the UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You mentioned that you were the chief UN Military Observer. Can you tell us who these military observers, commonly abbreviated as UNMOs, were?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: The UNMOs were -- first I must clarify that while I was chief UN Military Observer for Bosnia-Herzegovina, for administrative reasons, within the area I was known as the regional senior military observer for Bosnia-Herzegovina because there was an equivalent on the Croatian side. The UNMOs were military officers drawn from different countries of the world. While I was there, there were about 350 observers, approximately, drawn from around 38, 39 countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And these 350 observers were spread all over Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: They were spread all over Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, was there a specific unit that was focusing on Sarajevo, on the sector Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: Yes. The UNMO headquarters in Bosnia, that is, my headquarters, was divided into -- it had subunits; one based in Tuzla, which was called the Sector North; one in Sarajevo, which was called Sector Sarajevo; and one in the south, based in Konjic, which was called Sector South. Then I had a liaison officer, which was an extension of my own office. This was based in Pale. They were administratively and logistically -- logistically and operationally part of my own headquarters. Then we had teams in the enclaves; one was based in Gorazde, the other was in Zepa, and there was one in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I take it that you got information reports from all these UNMOs.

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: Regularly, yes. Twice a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So is it fair to say you had a fairly good take on what was happening not only in Sarajevo but also in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: In fact, the UNMO headquarters was the centre of all information that was flowing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you have a head UNMO who was in charge of Sector Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: Sector Sarajevo had a lieutenant colonel in command. They were -- I remember one of them, because it was a one-year rotation so people would change. I remember one of them was Colonel Mehboob from Bangladesh.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answer. Let's go now into various areas of experiences you made. You told us that you were in contact with the warring factions for various reasons. Now, let's first turn to the Bosnian army, the government's army, "ABiH," as it's commonly known. Did you have contact with liaison persons in the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: On the ABiH side there was one contact officer who was the liaison officer with us. His name was General Mustafa Hajrolahovic. I may be wrong in pronunciation. From the political side, from the government side, there was Mr. Hasan Muratovic. I think he was later the Prime Minister of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In terms of General Mustafa Hajrolahovic, did you have an opinion about his influence over military activities in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: I think he was very influential. He had been the corps commander of the Bosnian Sarajevo corps before he was assigned this assignment for liaison purposes. So he had a very good hold on whatever was happening in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember an incident when you saw shooting emanating from the sector, the UN camp area, and you tried to have it stopped?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: This incident did occur. Since the Serbs retaliated and a mortar shell fell near the French troops, therefore, I contacted General Mustafa and immediately got the firing ceased.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And just to make sure, who was firing from near the UN camp area?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: It was an ABiH mortar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me turn to the Bosnian Serb army whom you were also in touch with. Were you able to get into immediate contact with General Mladic upon your arrival?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: No. I had difficulties initially for about six weeks, four to six weeks, that I wasn't given an audience by Mr. Mladic, General Mladic, or General Karadzic. I think the arrival of the chief UNMO who was a Muslim was not liked by the team there. But over a certain period, I was able to establish a rapport with everybody and I could make my way to them. And on a number of occasions I subsequently saw General Mladic and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you have contact with senior officers of the Bosnian Serb corps around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: The direct dealing with these -- with the Romanija Corps, I think that was the name, the Romanija Corps, was by the Sector Sarajevo. But as the senior UN Military Observer in the region, I also -- in fact, initially when I arrived, I called on General Milosevic, who was the commander there. That was in the very first week or second week. And then subsequently a number of times I did visit the Romanija Corps; once specifically on the request of the senior military observer of Sector Sarajevo, Colonel Mehboob. And on other occasions also I did visit Lukavica barracks and, you know, the Romanija Corps headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Were there other officers from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps you remember having been in touch with during those times?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: Colonel Indic. He was -- because we had to deal with him on the movement of the convoys. And then he was probably the Chief of Staff, one of the senior staff officers, very influential. And whatever we wanted to get done, a word from Indic did move things. Then there was another gentleman. I think his name was Colonel Luganja. My pronunciation may not be correct. He was also there. He was a security officer or something, and I did come in contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We will get back to some of these gentlemen you mention in a moment, but let me turn to the overall picture in Sarajevo and perhaps in Bosnia. While you were in Sarajevo, Brigadier Mohatarem, was there shelling in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: I think shelling, it was so regular that if it was not there on a particular day you felt disturbed that something bigger is going to come subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what was shelled? Civilian areas? Military targets? Could you tell the Trial Chamber what you could observe and what reports you got from your subordinate UNMOs.

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: The exchange of fire continued on the confrontation lines between the two militaries, but the shelling was not so well aimed. It was targeted at civilians, and the number of casualties that would be on the UN record would indicate that civilians were regularly targeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who targeted the civilians? Who was the source of fire?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: The Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, could you, from your experience, distinguish a pattern of shelling of civilian areas in Sarajevo related to military activities or other activities that happened elsewhere in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: Shelling was a regular process, but it would increase in intensity if the Serbs wanted to make a point, or if they were serving as -- they were facing reverses somewhere in any of these sectors, the shelling would intensify. I must bring it to the notice of the Honourable Court here that Sarajevo itself was a kind of a theatre. I think the war in Bosnia by itself was the first war which was electronically transmitted the world over. Everybody saw it. What happened in Sarajevo was transmitted within minutes everywhere in the world; therefore, it was easier for anybody to, you know, to gauge the mood of the Serbs on a particular day, in terms of you could relate the shelling to what was going on in the other parts and what they wanted to convey to the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You told us a moment ago, Brigadier, that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was the source of fire. Now, who controlled these shelling activities, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: The commander of the Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, did you personally experience fire? Were you hit at any time during the time you were in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: I was -- a number of times I came under fire. My vehicle was hit once on the Igman road coming into Sarajevo from Kiseljak. And once my -- the aircraft I was travelling on with Mr. Akashi, coming from Zagreb to Sarajevo, that was hit. And I think another occasion my vehicle took a shell, a shell splinter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps if we could elaborate a bit more on these two examples. Can you tell us more about the aircraft you were travelling in with Mr. Akashi.

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: We were flying in from Zagreb in this aircraft. When it was coming in to land, it was hit by a 14.5-millimetre gun, an anti-aircraft gun, from the Serb side. It would be interesting to tell you that the next day, President Suharto from Indonesia was supposed to come in, and I was asked to convey to the Serb side that if anything happens to that aircraft, NATO would be let loose on the Bosnian Serb positions. And the next day the aircraft came in and it wasn't fired on at all, and Mr. Suharto came in and went out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You told us that you were asked to convey to the Serb side that if anything happens to that aircraft, NATO would be let loose on the Bosnian Serb positions. Do you remember to whom from the Serb side you relayed that message?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: I won't exactly remember, but I think I conveyed it to Colonel Indic on one side, in the Sarajevo Corps, and through my liaison team in Pale, I conveyed it to General Milutinovic, I believe, the Chief of Staff there in Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can I ask you, Brigadier, in the absence of the warning that you gave, in your view, was there a real possibility that the aircraft with General Suharto would have been fired on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was always the possibility, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because that would have been a civilian aircraft, would it not, or would it have been a military aircraft?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The aircraft that we were travelling in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, no, the aircraft taking General Suharto.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I won't remember. But the aircraft which I was travelling in, it was shot at at clear mark and view, and it was Mr. Akashi's personal aircraft that was recognised in the theatre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me go back, sir, if I may, to the other example you mentioned where you were personally shot at on the Igman route. Do you remember by -- and I think -- no, I don't think you mentioned. Do you remember what weaponry was used to shoot at you?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: It was a 14.5 anti-aircraft gun which was shooting at a fairly long distance. I couldn't see the gun, actually, because we used to move very fast on the Igman road, wherever the vehicle was exposed to firing. There was -- there were two portions on the Igman road where the vehicles were exposed to shooting from the Serb gunners.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the vehicle you were travelling with, can you tell Their Honours whether it was marked.

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: It was marked. It was a UN vehicle, white coloured, boldly written "UN," and it also flew a UN flag.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We were talking about shelling. Let's very briefly talk about sniping, Mr. Mohatarem. What experience did you and your subordinate UNMOs make about sniping during the time you were in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: Sniping happened mainly along the confrontation lines, and in the streets leading onto -- where there was a visibility for the snipers. There was a particular place which was called as "Snipers' Alley," which was the main road coming from the airport. I won't remember the name of that road. In front of the -- in front of the Holiday Inn, general area in front of the Holiday Inn, that was the main target, but all along the confrontation line. And most of the casualties or those that were hit by these snipers were civilian kids, women, old people who couldn't, you know, who couldn't move fast or who were unaware of these snipers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what was the source of this sniping fire?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: Sniping fire was from the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me move on to weapon collection points. Did the Bosnian army, the ABiH, have weapon collection points?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: Under the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement, there were common weapon collection points established for the ABiH and for the army of the Republika Srpska. There were two points for the ABiH. One was in the Tito barracks. This was manned by the Ukrainian battalion. And there was another in the tunnel beside the waterworks. I think it's Ciglana. I won't remember the name of the tunnel. Ciglana, I think. Ciglana tunnel. This was manned by the Egyptian battalion. There were five on the Serb side -- seven on the Serb side. There were five or seven, and they were all around Sarajevo. And the Serbs had very intelligently placed the weapon collection points, and even the weapons were placed in a manner that they could shoot from where they were. And they had minimum dislocation. Unlike the ABiH weapons, which were placed in a barracks and then in a tunnel, the Serb weapons were in the open and ready to shoot at any time from where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Did you or your UNMOs personally see the weapons collected at these weapon collection points of the Bosnian Serb side actually firing?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: I personally saw them firing. On a particular day, the UNMO team which was in the north had a very good OP from where -- observation point, from where they could see the Bare and Poljana weapon collection points. I saw a 122-millimetre gun also firing and I also saw a tank firing from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You mentioned in relation to the Bosnian army weapon collection points that they were manned by the Ukrainians and the Egyptians. What did you mean by "manned"?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: Manned is that these were -- they were assigned to protect these weapon collection points or secure them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was there also a unit from UNPROFOR who was assigned to the Bosnian Serb weapon collection points?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: There was a Russian unit which was assigned, and I think the French were also looking after one of the weapon collection points.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mohatarem. Just one point about rogue or irregular troops which are mentioned occasionally as playing a role in Bosnia. Do you have any comments on whether, on the ABiH side or on the Bosnian Serb side, there were any such rogue elements or irregular troops being active?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: I don't think so. There were no irregular troops. There was nobody outside the command of either the ABiH or the Romanija Corps. Everyone -- every soldier was accounted for, and he was directly responsible to his superiors for whatever he was doing. I don't believe that there were any irregulars or freelance operators there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned, sir, a few minutes ago that you met a couple of times with General Dragomir Milosevic, and I think that you mentioned that you were requested to come along with your Sector Sarajevo head of UNMO, the gentleman from Bangladesh, Lieutenant Colonel Mehboob. Now, can you tell us what was discussed during those couple of meetings between you and General Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: What we had done in the UNMO headquarters was that we had formulated a standard format for meetings with the -- both the ABiH and the Serb army. To start with, the format was, you know, we would lodge protests about sniping, about freedom of movement, about anything that we had concerns. They were conveyed, and that is -- I think this is exactly what I -- and the humanitarian convoys. I think this particular meeting was in relation to the movement of the humanitarian convoys as well as some shooting which was taking place, and the UNMOs were under threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And when you say that you lodged protests about sniping, what exactly do you mean?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: Sniping which was taking casualties of the civilians in the town, and we would go and lodge protests. There was one set of protests that I would file into Pale, and normally I wouldn't do it with the Romanija Corps, but it was on the request of -- because the colonel himself wanted this to look more important, this particular meeting, so he wanted me to go with him and I'd gone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. [Interpretation] Brigadier, you mentioned two meetings at least that you had with General Milosevic, and during these meetings you dealt, among other things, with sniping incidents. I'd like to know the following: When you talked to him about these sniping incidents, did he deny this, the reality of these sniping incidents, or did he accept that these facts, these events had taken place, or did he justify them by military necessity, or did he provide you with any other type of explanation? What did he say? What was his opinion about sniping?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of the time that we confronted the Serb commanders with information on this sniping or other violations they were rather dismissive about it. They won't accept that they had been shooting at civilians. They did accept that they'd been firing at their military counterparts. But exactly about the shooting at civilians, they were fairly dismissive about it. They didn't care about it, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me continue to a few events, Brigadier Mohatarem, that occurred from April onwards, 1995, about which I believe you do have knowledge. April 1995, do you remember attacks on UN personnel in Sarajevo, in Gorazde, and can you briefly tell us, if you may, what that was all about?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: The months of April, May, and June, I think, were the most difficult months during my tenure in Sarajevo. From the very beginning of April, the talks started that the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement is about to collapse or it will not be extended beyond the 1st of May; therefore, there were tensions. I remember that in early April - I won't know the dates - there were sniping incidents in which two French soldiers were injured. And in Gorazde, the Serbs who had -- in fact, from the very beginning of April, what they had done was that they'd stopped all humanitarian convoys and supply convoys for the UN also; therefore, there was a shortage of everything in Sarajevo and in the enclaves. In this period they were shooting at the British soldiers who were posted in Gorazde also. In fact, very interestingly, I asked my team in Pale to check up as to why they are shooting at the British, because they'd not done it before, and the answer that I got was that because of -- the Serbs saw the British riding mules and, you know, horses in that area, and that had happened because they'd run out of fuel. And so this is the logic they gave for shooting at the British. They didn't think they were the British soldiers. At the French, they'd done it, I think. It was first week of April. I won't know the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, sir. During April, and in connection with these French casualties, did you hear about a comment made by the brigade commander of the Ilidza Brigade?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: Yes. I was conveyed this by the commander of Sector Sarajevo that he had said they will get a dozen French for every Serb soldier who's killed. This is, I think, either preceding or after a Serb attack on one of the bridges, Vrbanja bridge, I think, where there were French soldiers. Two of them got killed. The Serbs also took away some of the soldiers; I won't remember the number. The French counterattacked and took the Vrbanja bridge and caused casualties on the Serb attackers also. And the Serb attackers were dressed in French uniforms when they attacked the French themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Going back to your UNMOs but still staying in April 1995, was there a hijacking of vehicles of your monitors?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: That was a regular phenomena there on the Serb side. The vehicles were hijacked. Slightly earlier than April, I think in February, March, I lost 11 vehicles. In April, I won't remember exactly, but I thought -- I think we lost one vehicle from our Pale team which was subsequently seen in convoys of the Serb leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And a related question; we haven't touched upon that: Did your subordinate UNMOs have freedom of movement; and if you can answer that question in both parts, in relation to whether they were stationed in the Bosnian Serb-held territory or in the territory held by the government forces? Was there freedom of movement for them?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: The freedom of movement of government forces -- government-controlled areas was generally there. There were certain areas they were sensitive to and they did prevent -- occasionally prevented the movement of the UNMOs. Otherwise, there was freedom of movement. In fact, most of the United Nations' presence was in the ABiH-controlled area and they had freedom of movement. On the Serb side, no, nothing of that sort. There was no freedom of movement. If there was movement allowed, it was very controlled. Like, if I was allowed to move around, I would have people trailing me and people ahead of me. It was just exactly -- if I'd given a timing that I'll move -- stay at this place at 11.00 to such a time, it was restricted to that, the routes, everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Brigadier. Let me move to an activity that occurred on the 16th and 17th of May, 1995. Do you recall an attack by the Bosnian Serb army on a feature Their Honours are already aware of, Debelo Brdo?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you tell Their Honours what this was about, how it developed over these couple of days?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: This incident was for -- the Serbs wanted to take -- there were two pimples or small hillocks which is entered there. That's why the name Debelo Brdo. These were overlooking the Miljacka river. Access -- control over this would have given them access or a direct line of site shooting ability to the Serb gunners at the centre of the Sarajevo town. And this they attacked with fire, mostly, with artillery fire, and they wanted to drive out the defenders from there. They didn't succeed. It was businesslike. It was directed at the defender -- within the confrontation line and directed at the defenders, but they couldn't dislodge them. It continued for two days, and after two days, the Serbs gave it up. But they came back, I think, after one week and tried to do the same thing again. This was -- the western side of Sarajevo town, the one on the west of the river, the Serbs had a traditional claim on that area and they thought that that was part of the Serb area, traditional Serb area, and they wanted it back.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you said a moment ago that they didn't achieve their aim to get this area back. Do you remember what happened, in your observation, after they realised they could not gain it through their actions, you described them as military actions?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: They rained Sarajevo town with artillery, with mortars; snipers were active all along the confrontation line. They took a fairly heavily toll on the civilians. I think in the month of May the civilian casualties were 70-plus killed and I think 250-odd injured. In those two days, I think they were very heavy on the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember an attack on one of the entries of the airport tunnel on the Butmir side that happened in early May 1995?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: There was an artillery shooting at the entrance of the Butmir tunnel on the Hrasnica side, and there I think 11 people were killed and, I don't know, I think 50-odd were injured in this. In fact, General Smith was very disturbed about this, and he discussed the possibility of a NATO attack on that particular occasion. But Mr. Akashi did not permit it and it did not take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you briefly address the issue of humanitarian aid convoys into the city? Were their check-points you had to deal with?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: All humanitarian convoys moving into Serb areas were managed through my office. We would be in -- we were the only office which was directly in contact on the Serb side. And we were dealing with Pale, not the Romanija Corps, in the context of the convoys. There were two check-points, S1, S4, and they created whatever difficulties they could. But generally if the -- after difficulties, the convoys were able to move if they were cleared by the army headquarters in Pale. There were cases where things were removed from the containers and, you know, the crews were robbed, but the convoys went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you tell Your Honours where these check-points S1 and S4 were located?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: On the northern side of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who manned those check-points?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: These were manned by the Romanija Corps. They were manned by the Romanija Corps. But the movement of the convoys were allowed or disallowed by Pale. Between the first week of April to June, I think, there were very, very few convoys. I had sent, I think, 195 requests or something and got clearance for five only. That caused a lot of hardship to the people, and it was a deliberate move to starve the people and to deny, even to the UN personnel, the resupply.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me move to a next topic, and we are almost at the end. This is air bombs. Are you familiar with the launching of air bombs at the time you were there in Sarajevo, in 1995?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: Yes. I've seen the air bombs. I've felt the air bombs. These were 500-pound aircraft bombs, and they had four 1.28-millimetre rocket motors [Realtime transcript read in error "mortars"], you know, screwed to them to give this 500-pound bomb flight. And these were fired from an improvised launcher which -- the rail that they prepared looked like an electronic pylon with crossbars, and that was placed on large trucks, and from that these were launched. I've seen one myself, this launcher, on the Pale road, and ...

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, but it seems to me that the witness did not say "rocket mortars" but "rocket motors." There's a difference between a mortar and an engine, a motor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said rocket motors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Motors?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: M-o-t-o-r.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's clarified. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did they have a sound, these weapons?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, you have it wrong on the -- as to what I said. "Motors," m-o-t-o-r-s. So let that be corrected.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't get your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I'll repeat it gladly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did these aerial weapons have a sound?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: They were very noisy weapons. I was having my lunch near the Presidency in a UN restaurant, and I just left that building when this weapon came with a whistling sound and exploded very heavily. All the -- in that particular restaurant where I just had food, all the windowpanes, et cetera, had broken down. And there were casualties this particular day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember the approximate, perhaps the exact, date of this incident?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: No, I won't. I won't remember that. I won't remember the date, the exact date. It should be in May or June somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And that's in 1995.

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: 1995. There were others also, because the two UNMOs got injured in Hrasnica, which is south of Sarajevo. This bomb had exploded and they also suffered injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And that's, again, this incident around that time frame, April, May, June.

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: Yeah, within this time frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned the attack you experienced yourself at the UN Presidency. Was that a military target?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: The UN building was not a military target. It was hit by a shell. One of the trees was chopped off. Luckily, it didn't hit the building. And we protested against this. General Smith himself signed the protest which was sent out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you described to Their Honours the make-up of these aerial -- these aerial weapons. Can you tell Their Honours, from your experience, could these be guided, could these be aimed at specific targets?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: They were not. They couldn't be aimed. They were free flight, and they were aimed to cause casualties wherever it hits. They were weapons which could not be managed. They could not be managed in terms of range. Direction -- general direction could be given to them, but they could fall anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And did you have a nickname for these bombs?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: These were called pigs, called pigs by the people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me move to the incident in August 1995 commonly referred to as the Markale market attack or massacre. Where were you at that time?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: I was outside Sarajevo. I was in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how were you made aware of the Markale attack?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: I was on the radio all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And did you initiate any actions after you heard about the attack?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: I wanted to get back to Sarajevo. I tried the French people who were guarding the Igman road. They did not allow a soft-top vehicle, and I was denied entry and I had to go back. Then the next day I requested for movement, and I couldn't even get on on the 29th. But on the 30th, early morning, I was specially provided an APC by the French, and I travelled -- I left my own vehicle in Kiseljak and came to Sarajevo in that APC. And I was immediately summoned to the BHC, which is the UNPROFOR headquarter, and I was briefed about it. I was asked about this very incident. Because what had happened was that once this incident took place, after the crater analysis were provided to the UNPROFOR head commander, he had requested for NATO air-strikes, but within 24 hours these strikes were called off. I think on the 30th they were called off. On the 29th, they started; on the 30th they were called off, because one of the senior UNMOs, a lieutenant colonel from Russia, he went to the press and public and he said that the firing had not been done from the Serb side. So there was a kind of embarrassment and the NATO attacks were halted. As soon as I came in, I was asked to reverify what had been provided by the UNMOs, because most of the crater analysis was generally done by the UNMOs. This decision was based partially on the analysis provided by the UNMOs. But I must also tell you that there were different people doing crater analysis there. There were the French engineers who would also go to the craters; there was the Bosnian police who would go to the craters; there was a team from the US embassy which covered important incidents. There was a British symboline, which is a piece of equipment, you know, mortar-tracking equipment, which also played a role. They also recorded the ingoing and outgoing weapons. And the French also had these recording devices, radar mortars, which were there. Everybody combined to come to a decision on this thing. It was not only one -- one, you know, one unit or the UNMOs alone who had come to this. But still, we were asked to do a -- redo this investigation. I had gone to the place, the site myself. I'd seen the crater myself. The team which had initially done -- which was -- the commander was -- the team leader was a Dutch officer, Colonel Konings, and he had done the crater analysis. There was some difference of opinion in the actual degree of entry, the hit that the round had taken. We had given 170 degrees and the others had -- one of the -- I must also add here, sorry to go back, there was a British --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Brigadier. I'd much prefer shorter answers, and I would ask the counsel to put specific questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you actually make a report about your findings?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: Yes. That is the -- I was asked specifically to give a report about the findings of the UNMO team, and I gave the report and placed the weapon which had fired on the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what was the basis for your information? You said you went to see the site, but you also talked to some people. What was the basis for your findings?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: The basis was physical. The UNMO team had done a professional job. And it was not only one round which had come into Sarajevo that day; there were five rounds. While the others concentrated on this round where a lot of civilians had got killed, we had done it for the other four rounds also. You could trace back the line of fire and trajectory, and we came to the conclusion that it was initiated from the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you have your report with you?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: I don't have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how big was your report?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: The final report that I gave to General Smith's staff was one page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me show you a couple of -- in fact, three documents, and that will then conclude the examination just before lunchtime. The first document is 65 ter number 198. If you could look at the --

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: I've seen this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. What is it?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: This is the report by the UNMO team leader, Colonel Konings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And that was the report you took into account when drafting your conclusions.

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May we have it enlarged.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Are you satisfied, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, it hasn't, but go ahead while it's being done.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honours, this report will play a control with several other witnesses. Colonel Konings will come himself and testify. The next -- if this report could be assigned an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P85, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If the next document could be shown. This is ter number 224. If it could be enlarged as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know what that represents?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: Yes, I do know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what is it?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: The UNMO headquarters report, Sector Sarajevo. This one is from Zagreb. Sorry. This one is from Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 20, the second part of page 20. "On the Federation Side ..." if that part could be enlarged. And perhaps I can read it slowly. "UNMO team Sedrenik was tasked to investigate the impacts in the general area of the marketplace (central city Sarajevo). The patrol carried out investigation in conjunction with sector engineers, the local civilian police and a local judge from Sarajevo court. The combined team conducted all investigations together, including visits to Kosevo and state hospitals to confirm dead, injured people." It goes on to talk about the crater analysis, and then at the end he talks about the impacts done by "120-millimetre mortar projectiles and the firing range, 170 MAG degree." Do you have a comment about that?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: This is the factual -- the report that is made by the UNMOs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Brigadier Mohatarem.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The last document, Mr. President, if it could be assigned a ter number as well. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit P86, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, may I ask you, are you bringing any evidence as to the total number of snipers that were engaged in this campaign?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We will bring evidence from a military expert who will talk about units that had sniping elements. We have documents that show that sniping training was conducted. Whether we can actually argue a final number I'm not sure about, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But I wonder whether the brigadier will have an estimate of the number of snipers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it would be difficult for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Difficult. Okay, thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The last document I wanted to show to the witness is ter number 269.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If you could have a moment to look at this document. It is drafted by General Nikolai and addressed to Mr. Rasim Delic. Please read it yourself. There is a second page which was attached to this document, and that's a document, a letter by Colonel Meille to Major General Milosevic. This is the second document, in essence, protesting about shelling and sniping of civilian areas. Have you seen these documents before?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen them. I don't remember them vividly, but such communication was -- I had access to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Is that an example of protests that were lodged towards the Bosnian Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how many of these letters are you aware of would have been filed during the time you were there as a senior military observer?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: Many, many. I don't think so -- I'll be able to recall, but I think in May we had eight or nine letters going out, in May alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If I can have a moment to consult with my colleague, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see it's time for the break. I may have one or two questions right after the break, and that will then conclude my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just put them now, or are you not ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I'd like to consult with my colleague before doing that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because I'm mindful of your urging us earlier to ensure that the brigadier leaves today.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm advised it will be no more than two or three questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll take the break now, and we'll resume at 2.00 p.m. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.47 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I just clarify that this afternoon we'll sit until 5.00 to ensure that the brigadier's testimony is concluded. In the event that it is concluded prior to that time, we will not begin the next witness, because it would not be productive to have the witness just for a few minutes. So you have a few more questions, just a minute or two?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. We have consulted over time. There are no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Then please begin the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. First, I wish to say that this morning we discussed an issue with the Prosecution concerning another witness who was to be examined today. We agreed that even had we sat all day today it would not have been possible to examine him because disclosure took place too late for us to be able to examine that witness. I will, of course, not abuse your patience, and I will try to be as efficient as possible today in order to conclude my examination as soon as possible. Does this suffice, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mohatarem, I am attorney-at-law Tapuskovic from Belgrade. I appear for the accused, Mr. Milosevic, and I wish to put some questions to you concerning issues of interest to the Defence. I will rely on the statement you made on the 11th and 12th of August, 1996, to the investigators of the Prosecution and only two documents. You will recall that on the 11th and 12th of August, 1996, you were examined immediately after the conflict in the area in question, and you may have been among the first witnesses to be questioned after the tragic events in Sarajevo. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: This is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: For this reason, I believe that your memory of the circumstances you were a witness to has remained fresh or, rather, was fresh at that time. So would you confirm that at the time you gave this interview you had a very good recollection of the events you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: Yes, I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In answer to Mr. Waespi's questions, you said - I cannot recall the exact words - something to the effect that Sarajevo at the time of these events, and especially during the time you were there but perhaps before that also, was a kind of stage for all the world and was a kind of media centre of the world. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: That would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Everything that happened in Sarajevo itself was very quickly learned by the whole world; perhaps sometimes on the same day. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, was anything known in the world about what was happening in the areas where the Serbs were? The whole world thinks or believes or is convinced or has evidence showing that the Serbs were firing, but they knew nothing in the centres of the important countries or, rather, their citizens knew nothing of what was going on on the other side.

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next two questions concern your profession. I won't dwell on it long. But as you're an expert for tanks, as far as I was able to understand, would that imply that you were fully familiar with the problems that exist in the case of other artillery weapons besides tanks?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: I generally know better about tanks than the other weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As, for the most part, you were a land officer, do you know anything about airborne bombs, any kind of bombs dropped from planes?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: Yes. I've undergone courses where I learnt about the different kind of bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But can you consider yourself a soldier who is an expert in such problems?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: I'm not an expert on air bombs, but I've learned during the course of my service. All land forces officers are also briefed or they undergo courses where they see airborne munitions also.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wish to rely on a certain document or, rather, on certain documents. One is the witness statement of the 11th and 12th of August, 1996. That's DD00-02-17. We had some problems with the electronic network this morning, but we have just been informed that it can, in fact, be used now. Do you see this statement, sir? Your statement, do you see it?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: No, I don't. Yes, I see the cover page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In order to conclude as quickly as possible, I would ask you to look at page 3 of the English version, towards the bottom of the page, where you are talking about your arrival in Sarajevo by plane. Have you found this?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: Yes, I do. With Mr. Akashi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Before I ask you something about this, could you tell the Chamber whether you met the accused? Is this him, Dragomir Milosevic, the accused? Could you confirm to the Chamber that he was the man you had contacts with?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: I did call on him, and I do recognise him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On how many occasions did you talk to him directly? Were you on your own in the delegation, were you chairing the talks with him, or was he just present there?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: No. I went with a delegation; I think two or three UNMOs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the page you see before you, you said -- rather, you gave an example, and you say that the fact that shots were fired on the plane in which Akashi and you arrived in Sarajevo, and this occurred in February, 1995, when you arrived; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: Not on that day, that particular day I arrived, but subsequently we'd gone to Zagreb and came back on the aircraft.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you that that's what it says here. So is what it says here incorrect?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: Yes, I was -- I was on the aircraft with Mr. Akashi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you say when you arrived in Sarajevo, after your plane landed, the day after -- it says here, "Mr. Soekarno" it must be "Mr. Suharto," was supposed to come to Sarajevo; is that correct? And then, "The day after," you say, "we conveyed to General Milosevic that if they fired at this aircraft, the whole NATO would come after them and nothing happened during this visit." My question is if you met Milosevic for the first time a week after this event, as you explained, how could you know that the shots were fired from the Serb side? And why did you not address both sides? Could you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: This was the professional opinion of the UNMOs who covered this shooting, that it was from the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you say, "We conveyed to General Milosevic." Who conveyed this? How do you know it was conveyed to General Milosevic and not to the Serb side in general? There were far higher ranking and more responsible on the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: It was conveyed on two levels; one was to Mr. Milosevic's headquarters through the Sector Sarajevo, and my own team at Pale also conveyed it to the army headquarters. That was the normal procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic was very rarely at Pale. He spent most of his time at the positions. So it would have been more normal to convey this to someone who made decisions at the top of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: It was conveyed to the top also, as I mentioned earlier, through the liaison team at Pale as well as through Sector Sarajevo to the Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, you spoke about the media in relation to Sarajevo. At the time you were there, did all these visits by eminent leaders, presidents, UN leaders at the time, mean that shots were often fired at the vehicles bringing these people to Sarajevo and that the Serbs were always suspected of doing this in the media, and that this was done the very same day the events occurred? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to move on and refer to certain events. I have to skip now to the last page of your statement where you mention Markale. I would very much like to clarify the Markale issue before the Chamber as soon as possible, so perhaps you can tell me something about it. You have already mentioned it when questioned by Mr. Waespi. On the last page of your statement, somewhere in the middle of the page, you mentioned the 28th of August. Have you found that place?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You say here that it was published on the 28th of August, that it was the Bosnian Serbs who were responsible for this shelling; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So what you just said happened again. As soon as the event occurred, on the same day, the Serbs were blamed before the whole world.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure whether that's what the witness statement says, and I'm not sure whether counsel is directing the witness to the statement or whether he wants to elicit the same information from the witness. The witness statement says on the 29th of August the announcement was made by the Bosnian Serbs, or that the Bosnian Serbs were responsible for that shelling. Just an observation from my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's only the date that you're questioning. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First, I should have -- well, I should have made a pause between what I read out and what I asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: First, Witness, I asked you to confirm whether it's correct or not that on the 29th of August, as it says in your statement, the announcement was made that the Bosnian Serbs were responsible for this shelling. You stated this in 1996. That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: On 29th August the Serbs were blamed for the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So my question is: As soon as the terrible event occurred, on the very same day, the Serbs would always be accused in definite terms of having done it, of being responsible; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the next sentence you go on to say: "General Janvier was also on leave that day, so General Smith decided to ask for NATO airstrikes." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: This is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The next sentence: "On the 1st of September, the bombing by NATO stopped due to declaration of a Russian colonel, Demurenko, that the shelling was not by the BSA, the Bosnian Serb army." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: Yes. This statement was made by Colonel Demurenko.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: He was the chief of that sector, a high-ranking Russian officer, Colonel Demurenko.

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: Yes, he was the chief of that sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And he was among the first to visit the site. Is that something you know about?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: No, he was not the first to visit the site. The team, led by Colonel Konings, was the first to visit the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct what you say next: "All agencies who made the first deduction about the origin of the fire, including my office, were ordered to conduct a new investigation, and for the moment the NATO air-strikes were put on hold."

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After that, your office conducted an investigation, is that correct, and determined that the mortar used was 120 millimetre? Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: Yes. We confirmed the findings of the investigation team.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No. It says here that your office, under your leadership, came to that conclusion. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: Yes. I came to that conclusion that the initial findings of the team were correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you then tell us when you first addressed General Smith? I understood you to say that it all started based on your report, the NATO activity.

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: As I spoke before, there were several agencies which conducted the crater analysis. Mine was one of them. And General Smith took a decision on the basis of the total picture that emerged in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I won't go back to that. There may be some minor discrepancies. But what I really want to ask you is something I have to ask, with the help of a document which is already in evidence here. 65 ter number 481.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter number 481, may this document be shown to the witness. It's a report dated the 28th, the day before the air-strikes began. The 28th, on the same day. Could the witness please look at the first page. Yes, this is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On the first page of this document, you see that on that first day General Janvier is reporting directly to Mr. Annan. Is that correct? Do you know about this report?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: No, I don't know about this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You never saw this report?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that the shell that was used was of 120-millimetre calibre weapon and that this was confirmed by your office.

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware, because you say you know about artillery, that mortar shells that -- rather, that it's very difficult to establish from where a mortar shell was fired, because it's impossible to establish the charge used to fire the projectile, and that this refers to the event of the 28th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the document I'm showing the witness, the document he's not aware of but which is dated the 28th, and it's on page 3 in the English version. UNPROFOR Sector Sarajevo. If the witness could read the passage where 120-millimetre calibre shells are mentioned. And he established that the mortar use was 120-millimetre.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't see that on the page that is open in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If I can assist, I think it's the previous page, page 2 of the actual document, because there is always a cover page. It starts -- so it's the previous page and it starts: "B. UNPROFOR: Sector Sarajevo," "(a) Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Towards the end of this paragraph, rather, halfway down the paragraph, it reads that in relation to that specific type of shell, it is very difficult to determine the positions for these mortar rounds because it is impossible to determine the level of charge used to fire the projectiles. My question is: Witness, do you know anything about this, anything about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi. Let's hear Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, it's a short paragraph, and I think it would be most fair that the whole paragraph, not just the second part, which I agree is most relevant for the Defence's point, but the whole -- because it, in fact, confirms about the calibre, these 120-millimetres. I think it would be fair. At least the witness has time to read the whole paragraph before addressing the second part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Let's give the witness a minute to read the paragraph in its entirety, and then you can put the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, sir, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Put the question now, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there is one remark that I would like to make. I will never ever, throughout this trial, try to use things out of context in order to lead the witness. It is precisely because of time. I think it would be an excellent idea if we had the time for every witness to go through the entire document before he's asked any questions at all; however --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think it would be a good idea to get on with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you know about this, what the document reads, something about a shelf of this kind as something that the artillery experts who wrote this - and these, in all likelihood, were top-notch experts, since they were acting on behalf of General Janvier - is it possible that they were entirely right in saying this? Or is it the case that you don't know about this particular feature normally displayed by this type of shell? Can you answer that one for me, please?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: Yes. There was no difference of opinion among all the five teams that conducted the crater analysis on the type of weapon used. Everybody -- nobody had a difference of opinion that it was 120-millimetre mortar. The difference of opinion was, as is evident, that in the degree of impact on the -- on the degree from which the shell had come.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you know that Colonel Demurenko, who, although he may have not been at the scene in the very first minutes, right from the outset, explained his position of the chance of a shell landing in that precise place was one against a million. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: No, that's not right, if the shell was given the correct trajectory. And these shells, there were five of them, they were not fired specifically at a particular target. They were generally fired in the area. And this particular one, the one which fell on the Markale market, took its toll. But, yes, in terms of the buildings that were around this, this shell had to be at a particular degree to have landed where it actually landed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no reason to keep you on this, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Brigadier, may I just ask you, the sentence: "The definition of firing positions for mortar rounds is very difficult, as it is impossible to determine the level of charge used to fire the projectiles." By the definition of "firing," is it meant the position from which firing took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, do you agree with that statement? What's your comment on that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, exactly pinpointing the position may not be possible, but the trajectory indicates that the distance that the fire -- the round took, this mortar took, was more than 2.000 metres. And that meant that it was on the Serb side. It was fired from the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just after the air-strikes started; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: The air-strikes started, after about 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Towards the end of the statement, you say: "On the 14th of September, the army of the Republika Srpska capitulated and pulled back." That's what you say. Back in 1996, you stated that, didn't you? So several months after the end of the war; right?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: This is on the 14th of September. The army of Republika Srpska agreed to pull out its heavy weapons from the zone which was earmarked earlier for safety of the people of Sarajevo. I may clarify here: There was a zone which was marked where heavy weapons could not be taken in, and these weapons, after the 14th of September, they were withdrawn by the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You stated in quite definite terms: "After the period of the NATO bombing there was little shooting in Sarajevo." Is that true, first of all?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So September, October, and November -- this is in reference to September, October, and November 1995. Would that be a fair assessment?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: Yes. The hostilities were very -- at a very low level in this period. This is the period where the -- the work-up to the Dayton Accord had started, and all the warring factions were, you know, taking that into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about the army of the Republika Srpska? Did they not face both NATO and the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina as enemies at the time?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: The enemies of Republika Srpska were the BiH army. NATO was there as the -- as the -- as the tool of the international community. And it was not an enemy of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I do understand that, but what I'm asking you is something else. In those situations, was the army of the Republika Srpska not facing both the BH army and NATO as opposition? You may or may not be able to answer, but what about most of the information about the positions held by the army of the Republika Srpska? Was NATO not being informed about those positions precisely by the BH army at the time?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: It's not correct. NATO had its own means. It had its --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness complete the answer. You asked the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: NATO had its own means. It had the satellites. It had other electronic devices, radars, which were watching the movement or the positions of the Republika Srpska army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In relation to that I have another question. This is page 2, the paragraph halfway down the page, that page of your statement. You talked about this a while ago while questioned by the Prosecutor, Mr. Waespi. I would like to go back to that now, given what I just heard from you. Have you got that there, sir? There's reference there to Mustafa Hajrolahovic. You tell a story there. On a day, the ABiH fired a mortar from the vicinity of the Zetra UN camp. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is plumb in the centre of Sarajevo; isn't it? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: It is. It is in the centre of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The Serbs fired back and one of their shells landed next to a UN base. Is that true as well, sir?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: That is true, and we protested to the BiH.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Just to be precise, the statement didn't say it landed next to the UN base. The statement says that their shells fell "in the UN camp." This is on page 2 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you. I think that's even more precise. Yes, that's right. I may have misread, but perhaps I wouldn't even be asking you this. You did talk about this when you spoke to Mr. Waespi. But the next passage, the next paragraph, about NATO, that's why I'm asking. That's the reason. The next example -- another example was during the NATO air-strikes, in the period end of August and beginning of September. This is poorly written. And then there's the example: "A Bosnian rocket-launcher fired from Sedrenik; nevertheless, the Bosnian government had agreed not to undertake any action during the NATO air-strikes." I'm not sure if I read this correctly. "They continued to operate, although they kept saying that there was no longer any need for them to operate." Can you please shed some light on this? I don't think there is any need for me to lead you on this. There is no need whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: They did fire a rocket and they were ticked off with that and that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me briefly, sir - maybe it's slightly beside the point - but do you know about the shells that, according to the indictment, fell on the TV building and the PTT building? Do you know about those bombs?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: Yes, I know about the bomb. On the PTT building, it was one of those 500-pound air force bombs. It fell next to the PTT building. And there was another one, which is the TV building, which is very close by to each other. But these bombs, as I pointed out earlier, they couldn't be aimed exactly at a target.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You've explained that, according to what you understand. I wouldn't dwell on that. We've heard enough on that. But do you know, sir, that there were quite a number of mortar positions occupied or held by the BH army around those buildings at the time? Is this something that you were aware of, or not?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: They may be -- they may be close to it. I exactly won't be able to comment on the exactly location of the BiH army positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like now to go to page 4, second paragraph of the English. There is some talk there of Srebrenica as well.

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It reads: "Sarajevo had a big significance. It was like a theatre for the world. Example: One week before the attack on Srebrenica, in July 1995, the Bosnian Serb army started with heavy indiscriminate fire on Sarajevo to attract the attention to Sarajevo and away from Srebrenica." Is my reading correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: My question: Was the BS army firing for that reason, or was, perhaps, July precisely the time of the most severe clashes between the two armies? I'm talking about July 1995, as well as June 1995. I see it says "July" here, but it started in June, didn't it? So above all, there were clashes in progress between the two armies after an offensive had been launched by the BH army, and Srebrenica in actual fact had nothing whatsoever to do with it.

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: I think the Serbs were shooting at Sarajevo to distract the international community from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I think I'm coming to something that is perhaps quite important. It's the same page, down towards the end of the page, and then it continues on the next page of the English statement. Have you got that, sir? It's the very last sentence of page 4. Well, there you go. There, you say, "In my opinion, the military targets in Sarajevo were," and then you go on to list some of those. Bullet 1, the battle locations and the confrontation lines and close to the confrontation lines. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: GHULAM MUHAMMAD MOHATAREM
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
